name: Antigone
role: Daughter of Oedipus, betrothed to Haemon
desc: The elder-seeming, fiercer daughter of Oedipus and Jocasta, niece of Creon. She buries her brother Polyneices against the royal edict, admits it without a tremor, and is walled up alive in a cave, where she hangs herself before the reprieve arrives.
why: I think she is right about the burial and hard to be near: cruel to her sister, half in love with death, and then, on the way to the cave, suddenly young and unsure. The play is better for refusing to make her a saint.

name: Ismene
desc: The sister who says no. She refuses to help with the burial because two women cannot fight the State, then tries to share the blame and the death once Antigone is caught, and is turned away by both her sister and, in the end, Creon.
why: She is the ordinary decent person in the play, and her argument for obedience is not contemptible. What happens to her offer in the Second Episode is the best evidence of how much Antigone's certainty costs the people who love her.

name: Creon
role: King of Thebes, brother of Jocasta
desc: Uncle to Antigone and king for a single day when the play begins, the brothers having killed each other. He forbids burial to the traitor Polyneices, condemns his niece for defying him, quarrels with his son and with the prophet, yields too late, and ends with son and wife dead by their own hands.
why: He begins with a defensible principle, that the city comes before kin, and I watch it shrink scene by scene into fear of being beaten by a woman. He is the one who changes, which makes the play at least as much his tragedy as hers.

name: Haemon
desc: Creon's last surviving son. He tries to talk his father round with tact and with the news that the city sides with Antigone, is called a woman's slave for it, and kills himself in the cave beside her body after lunging at his father and missing.
why: He makes the political case against Creon better than anyone, and never once says he loves her. Creon can hear nothing else, and that deafness is where the play turns.

name: Eurydice
desc: The queen, who appears only at the end. She hears the messenger describe her son's death, leaves without a word, and stabs herself at the household altar, cursing her husband as the killer of both her sons.
why: She has perhaps a dozen lines, and her silent exit is the most frightening moment in the play. She is the cost Creon never thought to count.

name: Chorus of Theban Elders
desc: The senior citizens of Thebes, summoned as the new king's trusted advisers. They sing the odes between scenes, defer to Creon while he is strong, pity Antigone without helping her, and find their nerve only after the prophet has spoken.
why: They are what a city sounds like when it is afraid of its ruler. I read their odes as aimed at Antigone and landing, every time, on Creon.

name: Teiresias
desc: The old seer, led by a boy, whose advice Creon has always followed until now. He reports that the altars are fouled with scraps of the unburied corpse, offers Creon a way to back down, is accused of taking bribes, and answers with the prophecy that Creon will pay with a child of his own.
why: He is the play's verdict. Until he speaks, Antigone's claim about the gods is only her word; after him it is a fact, and Creon collapses within a page.

name: Guard
role: A sentry set to watch the corpse
desc: A common soldier who draws the short straw to report the first burial, is threatened with torture, and comes back delighted with Antigone as his prisoner. He talks too much, hedges everything, and says openly that his own skin comes first.
why: He is funny, which matters in a play this bleak, and he is the honest measure of what most people do under a threat. Antigone looks stranger and braver standing next to him.

name: Messenger
desc: One of the king's men, who went with him to the plain and the cave. He tells Eurydice and the elders how Polyneices was buried at last, how Antigone was found hanged, and how Haemon died.
why: Everything violent in the play happens offstage and reaches us through him. His plain remark that a life without joy is a living death is the truest epitaph Creon gets.

name: Second Messenger
desc: A member of the household who comes out to tell Creon, already carrying his son's body, that Eurydice has killed herself indoors. He reports her last words, which lay both deaths at Creon's door.
why: He delivers the blow Creon did not see coming, and he does not soften it. The play ends with servants telling a king the truth.
